strengths: Presents a well-motivated, mathematically rigorous framework (Qronos) that provably unifies and generalizes two important prior rounding algorithms, OPTQ and GPFQ, by simultaneously handling weight/activation error correction and error diffusion.

Strong theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 3.2 rigorously connect the disciplined optimization formulation to an efficient Cholesky-based implementation, and Corollary D.1 gives a genuinely novel and interesting reinterpretation of OPTQ as correcting cumulative quantization error—likely of independent interest to the community.

Careful attention to computational practicality: derivation of a memory-efficient variant (O(N^2) vs O(mN)) is a nontrivial and useful engineering contribution, with concrete numbers (18x memory reduction, 13.8x runtime reduction) backed by microbenchmarks.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation isolating the rounding algorithm from the transformation stage across multiple bit-widths (1.58/2/3/4-bit), multiple transforms (SmoothQuant, MagR, HIP, QuaRot, SpinQuant), and both weight-only and weight-activation/KV-cache settings, showing consistent improvements over RTN/OPTQ/GPFQ.
Reasonable transparency about limitations (min-max grid only, 2x runtime vs OPTQ) and stated intent to open-source code.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted entirely to the Llama3 family (1B/3B/8B) and a single perplexity dataset (WikiText2) plus a small suite of zero-shot tasks; no evaluation on other model families (e.g., Mistral, OPT, Qwen) or larger-scale models (e.g., 70B) that would test generality of the improvements.

No direct empirical comparison to some of the most competitive recent rounding/quantization methods mentioned in related work (e.g., QuIP#, QTIP, AWQ, OmniQuant), even though these are discussed; the paper only benchmarks against RTN/OPTQ/GPFQ, making the 'state-of-the-art' claim only partially substantiated.

At extreme compression (1.58-bit), while Qronos improves over baselines by large relative margins, absolute perplexities remain very high (e.g., 34.8-79.5), and zero-shot accuracies stay near random-guess levels, raising questions about the practical significance of these particular results.

The paper acknowledges Qronos requires ~2x the runtime of OPTQ due to needing two forward passes (with/without quantization) to collect both X and Xe, which is a nontrivial practical overhead not deeply analyzed for larger models beyond the single microbenchmark and one anecdotal 1B-model runtime.

The empirical section reports single-run numbers without variance/confidence intervals across seeds for the main perplexity/accuracy tables (variance is only reported for the runtime microbenchmark), making it harder to assess the statistical significance of sometimes modest improvements (e.g., 4-bit results where gaps between Qronos and OPTQ/GPFQ are small).

strengths: Strong theoretical contribution: the paper provides a disciplined optimization formulation of PTQ rounding that explicitly handles mismatched input pairs (X, X-tilde), addressing both activation quantization and error propagated from earlier layers—an issue not explicitly formalized in prior GPTQ/GPFQ-style methods.

The equivalence proofs (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.2) that reduce a naively expensive per-column optimization to an RTN + Cholesky-based update are non-trivial and yield large practical gains (18x memory reduction, up to 13.8x runtime speedup), which is a genuinely useful systems contribution alongside the algorithmic one.

The reinterpretation of OPTQ/GPTQ (Corollary 3.4) as implicitly correcting cumulative quantization error via orthogonal projection is an interesting and novel theoretical insight that adds understanding to a widely used baseline, complementing concurrent geometric interpretations cited in the paper.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple model families (Llama3 0.6B-8B and larger, Qwen3 0.6B-32B), multiple bit-widths (1.58, 2, 3, 4 bit), weight-only and weight-activation/KV-cache settings, and multiple transformation techniques (HIP, MagR, SmoothQuant, QuaRot, SpinQuant, SmoothRot), with consistent and often substantial improvements over strong baselines (OPTQ, GPFQ, GPTAQ).

Careful experimental design isolating the rounding algorithm from the transform stage (fixing grid/transform and varying only the rounding method), which is a methodological strength not always present in prior PTQ papers.
Good reproducibility: code integrated into open-source Brevitas library, detailed hyperparameter ablations (e.g., SmoothQuant gamma, MagR theta, grid scaling beta) provided in appendix.
Honest reporting of limitations and negative results (e.g., GPTAQ instability/NaNs, overhead analysis showing decreasing relative cost with model size).
weaknesses: The runtime/memory benefits, while impressive on a single-layer microbenchmark, show a much more modest 8.7-19.7% calibration overhead versus OPTQ in the full-model Qwen3 experiments; the paper could be clearer up front about the more modest realistic overhead versus the flashier microbenchmark numbers.

Evaluation is limited to perplexity and 0-shot accuracy on relatively short/simple benchmark suites; no evaluation on larger downstream tasks (e.g., MMLU, generation quality, instruction-following degradation) which would better demonstrate practical significance of the perplexity/accuracy gains, especially at very low bit-widths like 1.58-bit where absolute performance is still close to random.

The comparison baselines (OPTQ, GPFQ, GPTAQ) are all sequential greedy rounding methods; no comparison to more recent gradient-based or learned rounding approaches (e.g., AWQ variants with joint calibration, OmniQuant-style learned quantization) is provided, which somewhat narrows the significance claims relative to the broader PTQ literature landscape.

Some of the gains at very aggressive bit-widths (1.58-bit) remain quite far from BF16 quality (perplexity still 18-40 vs. 6-9), raising questions about the practical usefulness of the method in that regime despite relative improvements over baselines.

The paper's contribution is somewhat incremental in algorithmic novelty relative to GPFQ/OPTQ—it is essentially a careful combination/generalization of existing greedy rounding ideas (path-following from GPFQ, weight update from OPTQ) with a clean mathematical formalization, and while the theoretical framing is valuable, the core algorithmic idea might be seen as an expected fusion of known building blocks.

Hyperparameter selection (e.g., dampening constant alpha, beta for grid scaling) appears tuned per setting, and while ablations are provided, it is unclear how sensitive Qronos's advantage is to careful hyperparameter tuning versus the baselines under equally careful tuning.

strengths: The paper generalizes prior greedy rounding methods (OPTQ, GPFQ) to explicitly handle the mismatch between original and (partially) quantized input activations, addressing a real and previously under-addressed source of error in multi-layer PTQ pipelines.

Strong theoretical development: the paper derives closed-form update rules, proves an equivalent and much more efficient implementation (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.2), and provides full proofs in the appendix rather than asserting results without justification.

The memory/runtime engineering contribution is concrete and impactful: reducing peak memory by 18x on Llama3-8B and up to 13.8x algorithmic speedup in a microbenchmark, with actual calibration runtime numbers reported on real models (Table 5).
The reinterpretation of OPTQ as an orthogonal-projection/error-correction procedure (Corollary 3.4) is an interesting byproduct that adds interpretability to a widely used baseline.

Experimental evaluation is broad: multiple model families (Llama3, Qwen3) and sizes, multiple bit-widths (1.58, 2, 3, 4 bits), multiple quantization transforms (SmoothQuant, MagR, HIP, QuaRot, SmoothRot, SpinQuant), and both weight-only and weight-activation/KV-cache settings, with a deliberate design to isolate the rounding algorithm's effect from the transform.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: integration into an open-source library (Brevitas) and a stated intent to release code/hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The practical gains are most pronounced only in extreme low-bit regimes (1.58-2 bit); at the more commonly deployed 3-4 bit weight and W4A4 settings, improvements over OPTQ/GPTAQ are often marginal (e.g., Table 3 W4 results, Table 4 W4A4KV16), raising questions about the real-world significance of the method outside of niche extreme-compression scenarios.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on WikiText2 perplexity and a fixed set of 5 zero-shot reasoning tasks; there is no evaluation on generation quality, instruction-following degradation, or more comprehensive benchmarks (e.g., MMLU), limiting confidence that improvements translate to broader downstream utility.

The method requires two forward passes (collecting both X and X̃) which adds non-trivial calibration overhead (up to ~20% for smaller models per Table 5); while acknowledged, this cost/benefit tradeoff is not deeply analyzed against the sometimes-marginal accuracy gains.

Some core building blocks are explicitly non-novel (the authors state Lemma 3.2 is likely already known, and the underlying alternating correct/diffuse structure closely parallels GPFQ and OPTQ), making the central algorithmic novelty largely a combination/generalization of existing ideas rather than a fundamentally new approach.

Baseline comparisons have reliability issues (GPTAQ produces NaNs in Table 4, and instability is only briefly footnoted), which complicates fair comparison and may affect the reported margins of improvement.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported across the many perplexity and accuracy numbers, despite several comparisons (e.g., between Qronos and GPTAQ/OPTQ at 4-bit) being fairly close, making the claimed 'consistent' superiority harder to fully verify statistically.

The claimed geometric/interpretability novelty (Theorem 3.4) overlaps with concurrent work (Birnick 2025; Chen et al. 2025) cited by the authors themselves, tempering the strength of the novelty claim in the abstract/intro.

The work is restricted to the scaled min-max quantization grid, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation; it remains unclear whether the reported gains would persist or shrink under more sophisticated/non-uniform grids used in some competing pipelines.
